demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: Meet Jack Harris, a 54-year-old forester who has spent his entire career working in the woods. He's been married to his high school sweetheart, Sarah, for over three decades, and they have two grown children together. On the surface, Jack's life appears idyllic, but beneath the façade lies a complex web of emotions and fears that have haunted him since a fateful day on the job. It happened five years ago when Jack was working as a team leader on a logging site. A younger colleague, Alex, was operating a chainsaw while Jack was guiding him from a distance. In a split second, Alex lost control of the saw, and it kicked back, severely injuring his leg. Jack was devastated by what he had witnessed and couldn't shake the feeling that he was to blame for not being able to prevent the accident. As time passed, Jack began to experience physical pain in his own body whenever he thought about the incident or encountered reminders of Alex. He would feel a sharp ache in his arm, as if he were reliving the moment when Alex's leg was injured. These somatic experiences left him on edge, making it impossible for him to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. The memories of that day continued to plague Jack, manifesting in vivid flashbacks where he felt like his body was reenacting the event. He'd be standing in the forest, and suddenly, he'd be back on that logging site, reliving the horror of what had happened. These episodes would leave him consumed by rage and grief, emotions so overwhelming that they made it difficult for him to breathe. Jack's fears extended beyond his memories, however. He began to feel threatened by strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations like walking down the street or shopping at the local market. He'd find himself watching people closely, scanning their body language for signs of potential harm. His inability to trust others was compounded by a deep-seated fear that he couldn't rely on himself. As Jack's anxiety intensified, so did his negative self-appraisals. He became convinced that there was something fundamentally flawed about him, something that had made the accident happen in the first place. This sense of intrinsic fault eroded his confidence as a forester and left him wondering if he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. Sarah, Jack's wife, noticed the change in her husband but struggled to understand what was happening. She'd try to reassure him that it wasn't his fault, that accidents happen, but Jack couldn't shake off the feeling of responsibility. As a result, he began to withdraw from social interactions and avoided going out with friends or family. The isolation took its toll on their marriage, and Sarah grew increasingly concerned about Jack's mental health. She encouraged him to seek help, but Jack was hesitant, fearing that therapy would expose his deepest fears and vulnerabilities. One day, while working in the forest, Jack came face-to-face with a stranger who reminded him of Alex. The encounter sent him spiraling into a panic attack, and for the first time, he realized that he couldn't keep living like this. He finally agreed to see a therapist, hoping to find a way to quiet his mind and learn to trust himself again. As Jack sat in the therapist's office, he felt a mix of emotions: anxiety about facing his fears, but also a glimmer of hope that maybe, just maybe, he could learn to live with himself again. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but for the first time in years, he felt like there was a possibility of redemption, of rediscovering the man he used to be before that fateful day on the logging site.
